extracted.intended_audience: sitcom/TV comedy writers and writers' room staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating, improving, and structuring jokes and scene endings in a television sitcom writers' room. Focuses on predictability, punchlines, 'like-a-jokes', beats, buttons, toppers, and tactics to strengthen humor before lock-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 2's
rubrics_metrics.description: If any two writers pitched essentially the same punchline, they discarded it — even if funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: if two writers came up with the same joke, audience members likely will too. Predictable jokes don't land as hard. Anti-pattern: keeping a punchline that multiple writers independently thought of, because that increases the chance it will feel obvious to viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Questions for Every Joke
rubrics_metrics.description: For every joke pitched, ask: (1) Is it funny? (2) What would be funnier?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't accept your first answer; always push to make it funnier. Do not 'pat yourself on the back' after the first test — treat the second question as a mandatory push to improve the joke before locking it in.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Like a Joke"
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Like a joke' has the rhythms of a joke but is not funny — just a straight sentence delivered as a joke line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cadence/structure tricks people, but there's no actual punch. Anti-pattern: keeping lines that sound jokey but lack a payoff; ruthless writers cut these. Use this as a diagnostic to remove lines that merely imitate joke rhythm without delivering humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beating Jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly try to 'beat' (replace with a funnier version) every joke before lock-in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make iterative attempts to find stronger punchlines; treat every joke as improvable. Procedural tip: solicit alternate phrasing or setups in the room until a superior version emerges; do not finalize a joke until no one can beat it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 1: Tested against 'what would be funnier' question
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the joke been tested against the 'what would be funnier' question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the Levine Method rubric — ensure the joke survived deliberate attempts to improve it. If you can't articulate a plausible 'funner' alternative, that may indicate you've pushed far enough; otherwise keep searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 2: Predictability / Two-writer duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Could two writers easily pitch this — i.e., predictable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple writers independently devise the same punchline, reject it as too predictable. This criterion operationalizes the Rule of 2's: seek originality to avoid jokes that audiences will also predict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 3: Real joke vs. 'like-a-joke'
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it a real joke or a 'like-a-joke'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose lines that have joke form but no actual payoff and cut them. Use this to filter out cadence-only lines that give the illusion of humor without the substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 4: Scene has a strong button
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the scene have a strong button?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A button is the final joke of a scene — it should land and close the scene effectively. Evaluate whether the button is the blow or a strong closer that leaves the audience satisfied; revise if the scene ends weakly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 5: Presence of toppers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topper = a tag that beats the previous joke. Include or develop toppers that escalate or outdo the preceding punch when appropriate. Toppers can increase momentum and raise the laugh level after an initial punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats: events that occur in a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and map beats to structure scenes and place jokes at effective moments. Use beats to time setups and callbacks; ensuring clear beats helps jokes land within the scene's rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savers
rubrics_metrics.description: Savers: damage control jokes right after your real joke pitch dies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare savers to recover momentum if a primary joke fails in the room or on stage. These are short fallback jokes that can repair or redirect the scene when an intended punch doesn't land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Button (term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Button: final joke of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A button should be strong and definitive. When evaluating scene structure, ensure the button closes the scene and leaves a laugh or beats the emotional note you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swinging in on a rope
rubrics_metrics.description: "Swinging in on a rope": side character enters, delivers a joke, leaves (used in CHEERS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this device to get cheap, sharp jokes from secondary characters without changing scene focus. Consider it as a tool to insert jokes without disrupting main beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow
rubrics_metrics.description: Blow: the strongest joke that ends a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and place the 'blow' where it will have maximal impact — often at scene end. Distinguish between smaller jokes and the blow so you can structure escalation properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topper (term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topper: a tag that beats the previous joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topper should be an intentional escalation; evaluate whether a topper improves the laugh or merely dilutes the prior punch. Use toppers to lengthen or heighten a joke beat when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch (term)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch: an idea suggested in the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present pitches concisely and be prepared for rapid testing and beating. Pitches are the starting point for the iterative process — expect them to be challenged, refined, or discarded.
